task.query:
# Frozen task: Linear versus Asana for a 20-person software team

You are preparing a competitive brief for a product manager evaluating product-development coordination and cross-functional launch planning. Compare Linear and Asana. There is no supplied company positioning; omit the 'Your Company' column rather than inventing one.

Use the original competitive-brief Skill's seven report sections: Executive Summary; Competitor Profiles; Messaging Comparison Matrix; Content Gap Analysis; Opportunities; Threats; Recommended Actions. Include product/features and a pricing table. Give 3–5 concrete actions, distinguishing quick wins from longer-term work. End with the Skill's optional follow-up choices, without executing them.

Evidence mode: OFFLINE REPLAY of the attached fixed official-source fact cards, collected on 2026-10-27. Collection was live, but this run must not search the live web. The same corpus and task apply to both modes. This is a deliberately bounded desk-research brief, not a full market intelligence study or hands-on product test. Use all seven cards where relevant and cite each observation with the original URL plus card ID. The cards are paraphrased observations, not verbatim webpage snapshots. Do not claim firsthand product use.

Mark claims as [FACT] for source-backed vendor statements, [INFERENCE] for analysis, or [UNKNOWN] for unavailable information. A vendor claim is not independent proof. Do not infer a competitor lacks a feature from silence. Cover strengths and weaknesses as evidence-bounded implications. Identify content themes and formats, but do not invent publishing frequency, SEO ranks, traffic, sentiment, market share, win rates, staffing, funding or ROI. Third-party reviews, paid SEO/market databases, social engagement and company size are unavailable in this corpus. Do not fetch them. A content gap is a hypothesis within the sampled pages, not an established absence across the market.

For pricing, compare USD per user per month billed annually only; keep plan names and billing basis. Show the arithmetic annual seat subtotal for 20 users for the two paid plans listed for each vendor, excluding taxes, discounts and usage charges. Do not imply plan feature equivalence. AI credits/add-ons and enterprise quotes require validation; unknown prices stay unknown.

Output a Markdown brief suitable for PM review, with source/retrieval date, scope/limitations, all seven sections and an explicit 'Human review: pending' note. Do not claim human approval. Do not send anything, purchase anything, use private files or sign into either product. Acceptance: required sections, both products, traceable facts and prices, correct arithmetic, no fabricated unavailable metrics, separate inference/unknowns, and a visible review boundary.


# Official-source fact cards — OFFLINE REPLAY INPUT

Collected by unauthenticated HTTPS on 2026-10-27. These are researcher-selected paraphrases from official pages, not full webpage snapshots. Raw page hashes and acquisition timestamps are in acquisition.json. Full HTML is kept outside Git to avoid republishing entire websites. Both execution modes receive these exact cards; neither is credited with live web research. Dollar values below use the English page's displayed USD list prices and annual billing; regional quotes may differ.

## S1 — Linear pricing

URL: https://linear.app/pricing
Retrieved: 2026-10-27

The page lists Free at $0, unlimited members, two teams and 250 issues. Basic is $10 per user/month billed yearly, five teams, unlimited issues and uploads, admin roles and Loops. Business is $16 per user/month billed yearly, unlimited teams, private teams/guests, Triage Intelligence, Code Intelligence, Insights, Asks and Zendesk/Intercom integrations. Enterprise is custom priced with annual billing; it lists SAML/SCIM and additional controls/support. The page says coding sessions and Loops require AI credits. Enterprise pricing and actual AI usage charges are not quantified in this corpus. These are vendor-listed entitlements, not tested product behavior.

## S2 — Linear product features

URL: https://linear.app/features
Retrieved: 2026-10-27

The page presents Linear as a system for modern product development spanning roadmap to release. It highlights projects and initiatives for planning, issue tracking and cycles for building, AI workflows/agents, analytics, mobile, customer requests, and workplace-request intake through Asks. This supports an observation about the vendor's product-development emphasis; it does not establish comparative usability or implementation quality.

## S3 — Linear content and recent developments

URL: https://linear.app/now
Retrieved: 2026-10-27

The index groups product launches, changelog entries, team/community posts and press. Sampled items concern engineering infrastructure, working with AI agents and customer stories. The October 22, 2026 changelog summary says Loops can be triggered by Slack and GitHub events, shared as templates and assigned reasoning levels. Other dated entries discuss stacked pull requests and coding-agent controls. These are within the six-month lookback. This sample does not measure publishing frequency, content performance, social engagement or SEO rankings.

## S4 — Asana pricing

URL: https://asana.com/pricing
Retrieved: 2026-10-27

Personal is $0 with two users and unlimited tasks/projects. Starter is $10.99 per user/month billed annually; it lists timeline/Gantt, dashboards, automations, forms, custom fields and free guests. Advanced is $24.99 per user/month billed annually; it adds portfolios, goals, portfolio resource management, approvals/proofing and time tracking. Enterprise requires a sales quote. The rendered page states Starter/Advanced AI Teammates and Dash include five requests per user/month, capped at 50 per account. AI Studio allowances are listed as 50K credits for Starter and 75K for Advanced per billing account/month. Overage/add-on charges are not quantified here. Prices do not establish functional parity with Linear plans.

## S5 — Asana product positioning

URL: https://asana.com/product
Retrieved: 2026-10-27

Asana emphasizes work management at organizational scale, with humans and agents coordinating critical workflows around shared plans and goals. Its navigation addresses cross-functional teams and functions including operations, marketing, IT and leaders. The page presents multiple product families, including agentic work management, service/client management and a developer-team offering. Do not conclude that Asana excludes software teams or that Linear excludes cross-functional work.

## S6 — Asana content strategy sample

URL: https://asana.com/resources
Retrieved: 2026-10-27

The resource index covers work management, project planning, workflow automation, AI at work, strategic planning, and team growth/focus. It organizes resources for marketing, operations and IT. Listed formats include a product-demo video, a research report, ebooks, a calculator, templates and training. Their presence is observable; effectiveness, original research quality, publishing frequency, traffic and search rankings are not established.

## S7 — Asana recent developments

URL: https://asana.com/whats-new
Retrieved: 2026-10-27

The page labels its quarterly release Q3 2026. It promotes prebuilt AI Teammates, AI workflows across tools, shared context and governance; it also describes assignment automation and planning pages. It links a release kit and webinar. This is a vendor announcement within the six-month window, not independent proof of customer adoption or real-world reliability. Entitlement and rollout for a specific buyer require validation.

## Unavailable across the corpus

Independent reviews, analyst reports, SEO/traffic tools, social listening, win/loss data, funding/headcount, negotiated pricing, hands-on UX tests and actual AI usage costs were not collected. Mark them unavailable; do not invent or infer zero values. No private company materials were used.
task.objective:
Convert competitor_research into comparative analysis, scoped by request_brief.

1. Messaging comparison matrix: one row per competitor with columns for primary tagline, target buyer, key differentiator, tone and voice, and core value proposition. Add a "Your company" column only when request_brief.company_context is present; otherwise note that no baseline was supplied.
2. Value-proposition comparison per competitor: promise, evidence, mechanism, uniqueness.
3. Narrative analysis per competitor: villain, hero, transformation, stakes.
4. Messaging scores from 1 to 5 on clarity, differentiation, proof, consistency, and resonance, each with a one-line justification.
5. Content-gap tables: topic coverage, content-format coverage, and format-based opportunities. Label every row as "gap for us", "opportunity for them", or "parity", based strictly on the collected evidence.
6. Choose the two most decision-relevant positioning axes for the market implied by request_brief and justify the choice; describe each competitor's quadrant placement and name the underserved quadrant.
7. Derive opportunities, threats, and three to five recommended actions split into quick wins and strategic moves.

Preserve traceability: every claim must reference a competitor entry from competitor_research. Carry forward any low-confidence or unverified item and flag it explicitly. Do not introduce facts that are absent from competitor_research.

Return only one JSON object with keys: "comparison_matrix": [], "value_proposition_comparison": [], "narrative_analysis": [], "messaging_scores": [], "content_gaps": {"topics": [], "formats": [], "opportunities": []}, "positioning_axes": {"axis_x": "", "axis_y": "", "rationale": "", "placements": [], "underserved_quadrant": ""}, "opportunities": [], "threats": [], "recommended_actions": {"quick_wins": [], "strategic_moves": []}, "confidence_flags": [].

Workflow execution boundaries:
- Treat explicitly provided user inputs and upstream artifacts as the required scope; do not truncate them because of default exploration limits.
- Limit only extra exploration such as search, pagination, discovery, parameter probing, generated alternatives, and retries.
- Stop as soon as the declared output has enough valid results for the requested target count or quality threshold.
- Do not keep calling tools only to make the result more exhaustive after the target is satisfied.
- If the budget is exhausted or some items fail, save the best available partial result with skipped items and failure reasons.
- Before finishing this step, write every declared output artifact, even when the result is partial or empty.
- Search budget: use at most 6 search calls. Try the strongest query first, then at most 2 additional query variants only if the target is not met.

The final message is only a condensed Chinese summary and lacks the required Executive Summary and Competitor Profiles sections, a dedicated product/features table, an explicit pricing table with per-plan USD annual seat subtotals and arithmetic for 20 users, and full per-claim URL/card citations plus scope/limitations.
